about:
**if you want to go fast, go deep first.** pstack is the skill set that [poteto](https://x.com/poteto), Lauren Tan of the React core team, uses to ship at Cursor. Its goal is less code of higher quality, so you can run many agents in parallel and trust each one.

### How it works

You start every rigorous task with one router, `/poteto-mode`. It reads the request, matches it to one of 23 playbooks such as bug fix, feature, investigation, babysit, or shipping, and copies that playbook's steps into a todo list. As each step fires, the router loads the skill the step needs. `how` and `why` investigate, `architect` and `arena` compare designs, `swarm` verifies, and `unslop` edits prose. Each decision names the principle behind it, such as *Laziness Protocol* or *Prove It Works*, so a reviewer can check the choice against that rule.

pstack splits work by model strength. Routine code goes to a fast code model. The hardest changes, prose, and judgment go to the strongest model.

### Get started

```
/plugin marketplace add cursor/plugins
/plugin install pstack@cursor-plugins
```

Run `/setup-pstack` once to pick models, then start a task with `/poteto-mode <task>`.

### In this deck

♠ is the router, ♥ are its playbooks, ♦ are the skills they call, ♣ are the principles they cite, and ★ are the subagents.

cards.name: architect
cards.title: Architect
cards.description: Sketch types, signatures, and module structure before code, then stay in the loop while implementation fills in. Use for /architect, 'architect this', 'design this', or non-trivial work where jumping to code would lock in the wrong shape.

cards.name: arena
cards.title: Arena
cards.description: Spawn N parallel candidates at the same task, pick a base, graft the strongest parts of the losers into it. Use for /arena, 'arena this', 'throw it in the arena', or when one attempt at a non-trivial artifact would lock in the wrong shape.

cards.name: automate-me
cards.title: Automate me
cards.description: Use for "automate me", "create/update/refresh my -mode skill", "turn/capture my preferences or working style into a skill", or wanting agents to follow how the user works. Drafts or revises a personal -mode skill via create-skill + unslop, optionally pulling fresh evidence from recent transcripts.

cards.name: benchmark-checklist
cards.title: Benchmark checklist
cards.description: Vet a perf measurement (limiter, tuning, limits, errors, repeatability, relevance, and whether the work happened) before you report or act on it. Use when you run a benchmark or report a speedup or regression you measured.

cards.name: blast-radius
cards.title: Blast radius
cards.description: Find what a change could break somewhere else before it ships, beyond the diff, and prove the one fact it's safe because of by running real code instead of writing it up. Use for 'blast radius of X', 'what could this break', or reviewing a small diff you don't trust.

cards.name: bro
cards.title: bro
cards.description: Restate the last message in plain human language, with no jargon.

cards.name: correct
cards.title: Correct
cards.description: Find the mistakes agents keep repeating in this repo and make each one impossible. Try architecture first, then types, then a lint whose error names the fix, then a test, and write docs last. Prove each check fails on a real past mistake. Repeat this each time the operator corrects you. Use for /correct.

cards.name: create-formal-verification-skill
cards.title: Create a formal verification skill
cards.description: Generate a project-local skill that formally verifies the code where a bug costs the most and tests reach the least, in any language, with whichever verification tool fits. Use for /create-formal-verification-skill, "model-check this race", "prove this invariant", or when concurrency, retries, state machines, parsers, or unsafe code need more than tests.

cards.name: create-verification-skill
cards.title: Create a verification skill
cards.description: Generate a project-local verification skill that drives your app the way a user does — any language, framework, or platform. Use for /create-verification-skill, "make a control skill for this repo", or when a project has no scripted way to prove UI/CLI/service behavior.

cards.name: figure-it-out
cards.title: Figure it out
cards.description: Design an auditable playbook when no narrower one fits: a large migration, an ambitious multi-part change, or work a human reviews after stepping away. Scales rigor to the task, runs a hypothesis loop, and logs decisions. Use for /figure-it-out or 'figure it out'.

cards.name: how
cards.title: How
cards.description: Use for "how does X work", code walkthroughs before changing something, and placement / ownership / layering questions ("where should this live", "which package owns this", "is this the right layer"). Explains subsystem architecture, runtime flow, onboarding mental models. Use why for motivation.

cards.name: in-your-own-words
cards.title: in-your-own-words
cards.description: Restate in your own words what you think the user's goals are and what problem they're trying to solve. Use for /in-your-own-words.

cards.name: interrogate
cards.title: Interrogate
cards.description: Use for "interrogate", "adversarial review", "multi-model review", "challenge this", "stress test this code", "find blind spots", or "tear this apart". Adversaries try to break a change or design, and only findings proven by a run survive.

cards.name: ketchup
cards.title: Ketchup
cards.description: Catch the user up on what changed in this chat since their last message, in plain words and small visuals. List every item waiting on them with what they need to decide it from the reply alone. Use for /ketchup.

cards.name: ketchup-video
cards.title: Ketchup video
cards.description: Catch the user up like /ketchup, with a short subtitled video of slides for what happened and the waiting calls as text under it. Use for /ketchup-video.

cards.name: maintain-formal-verification-skill
cards.title: Maintain a formal verification skill
cards.description: Bring a project's formal verification back in line with the code after the code changes: find the commits that touched verified code, update the model, harness, or properties to describe the code as it is now, rerun, and say whether each failure is drift in the verification or a bug in the code. Use for /maintain-formal-verification-skill, "is the model still true to the code", or after merges and refactors that touched verified code without rechecking it.

cards.name: maintain-verification-skill
cards.title: Maintain a verification skill
cards.description: Periodic pass that keeps a project's verification skill and feature map honest: parallel source readers per feature, one live session driving every feature, at most one PR of proven corrections. Use for /maintain-verification-skill or "audit the verify skill".

cards.name: make-bot-ui
cards.title: How to make a bot UI
cards.description: Use when building a custom UI (page, dashboard, buttons) that should wake a Grok Bot over a webhook, when the user must provide a webhook sender key, or when exposing that UI on Tailscale.

cards.name: no-comments
cards.title: No comments
cards.description: Spawn Comment Sicko, fix accepted findings, and offer encodings for claimed constraints.

cards.name: poteto-help
cards.title: Poteto help
cards.description: Guides users through pstack setup, /poteto-mode, and picking the skill, playbook, or principle for a task. Type /poteto-help with a question.

cards.name: poteto-mode
cards.title: Poteto mode
cards.description: poteto's agent style for concise, detailed responses, deliberate subagents, unslopped prose, simple code, and verified work. Use for poteto, /poteto-mode, or requests to work in this style.

cards.name: attack-the-premise
cards.title: Attack the Premise
cards.description: Apply when two or more fixes that share one premise have failed the same gate. Write the premise down and test it directly before you write another fix that assumes it.

cards.name: boundary-discipline
cards.title: Boundary Discipline
cards.description: Apply when wiring validation, error handling, or framework adapters. Concentrate guards at system boundaries (CLI, config, network, external APIs); trust internal types and keep business logic in pure functions.

cards.name: build-the-lever
cards.title: Build the Lever
cards.description: Apply to any non-trivial work, not just bulk work: edits, migrations, analyses, checks. Build the tool that does it or proves it (codemod, script, generator, or a skill your subagents follow) instead of working by hand. The tool is the artifact a reviewer can rerun.

cards.name: encode-lessons-in-structure
cards.title: Encode Lessons in Structure
cards.description: Apply when you catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time, or notice a recurring correction. Encode the rule as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check, or script instead of more text.

cards.name: exhaust-the-design-space
cards.title: Exhaust the Design Space
cards.description: Apply when facing a novel UI interaction or architectural decision with no precedent in the codebase. Build 2-3 competing prototypes and compare side by side before committing.

cards.name: experience-first
cards.title: Experience First
cards.description: Apply when product, UX, or feature-scope tradeoffs come up. Choose user delight over implementation convenience; ship fewer polished features over more rough ones.

cards.name: explain-the-number
cards.title: Explain the Number
cards.description: Apply before you measure, and before you trust, report, or act on a number you measured: a speedup, a regression, a throughput, a latency, or an eval result. Find what limits it, and rule out that it measured something other than the work you think.

cards.name: fix-root-causes
cards.title: Fix Root Causes
cards.description: Apply when debugging. Trace each symptom back to the first place the system went wrong and fix it there. A guard is a fix only when the state it handles is legitimate.

cards.name: foundational-thinking
cards.title: Foundational Thinking
cards.description: Apply before writing logic: choosing core types and data structures, sequencing scaffold-vs-feature work, asking what concurrent actors share. Get the data structures right so downstream code becomes obvious.

cards.name: guard-the-context-window
cards.title: Guard the Context Window
cards.description: Apply when context is filling up: large outputs, long files, repeated reads, fan-out planning. Route bulk to subagents; keep summaries in the main thread, not raw payloads.

cards.name: laziness-protocol
cards.title: Laziness Protocol
cards.description: Apply when refactoring, evaluating diff size, or tempted to add abstractions, layers, or signal threading. Bias toward deletion and the smallest change that solves the problem.

cards.name: make-operations-idempotent
cards.title: Make Operations Idempotent
cards.description: Apply when designing commands, lifecycle steps, or processing loops that run amid crashes, restarts, and retries. Converge to the same end state regardless of partial prior runs.

cards.name: migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis
cards.title: Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs
cards.description: Apply when introducing a new internal API while old callers still exist. Migrate callers and delete the old API in the same wave instead of preserving compatibility layers.

cards.name: minimize-reader-load
cards.title: Minimize Reader Load
cards.description: Apply when reviewing or shaping code that's hard to trace. Count layers between question and answer, and hidden state in the reader's head; collapse one-caller wrappers and shrink mutable scope.

cards.name: model-the-domain
cards.title: Model the Domain
cards.description: Apply when writing stateful logic, or when code branches a lot or repeats a shape assumption across files.

cards.name: never-block-on-the-human
cards.title: Never Block on the Human
cards.description: Apply when tempted to ask 'should I do X?' on reversible work.

cards.name: outcome-oriented-execution
cards.title: Outcome-Oriented Execution
cards.description: Apply during planned rewrites and migrations with explicit phase boundaries. Converge on the target architecture; don't preserve smooth intermediate states with throwaway compatibility code.

cards.name: prove-it-works
cards.title: Prove It Works
cards.description: Apply after completing a task, before declaring done. Verify against the real artifact (run the feature, read the actual value, inspect the diff), not a proxy, self-report, or 'it compiles.'

cards.name: redesign-from-first-principles
cards.title: Redesign From First Principles
cards.description: Apply when integrating a new requirement into an existing design.

cards.name: separate-before-serializing-shared-state
cards.title: Separate Before Serializing Shared State
cards.description: Apply when concurrent actors might write to the same file, branch, key, or state object. Eliminate the sharing first; serialize structurally only when one shared writer is a real invariant.

cards.name: sequence-verifiable-units
cards.title: Sequence work into verifiable units
cards.description: Apply to multi-step work (sweeps, migrations, runs of similar edits) and to how you stack commits and PRs. Break work into small units that each end in a verifiable state, check each before the next, and order delivery so the sequence proves itself to a reviewer.

cards.name: subtract-before-you-add
cards.title: Subtract Before You Add
cards.description: Apply when sequencing an addition, refactor, or rewrite. Remove dead code, redundant validators, and stub references first, then build on the simpler base.

cards.name: test-behavior-not-implementation
cards.title: Test Behavior, Not Implementation
cards.description: Apply when you write, change, or keep a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so that the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change.

cards.name: type-system-discipline
cards.title: Type System Discipline
cards.description: Apply when designing types, reviewing a function signature, or writing code in any statically-typed language. Make illegal states unrepresentable, brand semantic primitives, parse external data at boundaries, exhaust variants, derive from authoritative schemas.

cards.name: recall
cards.title: Recall
cards.description: Reconstruct your recent working context from your own chat history, live state, and the shared record (user reports, prior fixes, incidents), then hand back a tight current-state brief. Use for 'recall my work on X', 'catch me up', 'what have I been working on', 'where did I leave off', before starting or resuming work.

cards.name: reflect
cards.title: Reflect
cards.description: Spawn three parallel review subagents over the active transcript, surface learnings, and route each to a concrete edit on an existing skill. Use when the user says reflect.

cards.name: setup-pstack
cards.title: Setup pstack
cards.description: Configure which models pstack uses per role and at what reasoning budget. Detects your available models and writes an always-applied rule that overrides the skill defaults. Use for /setup-pstack, "configure pstack models", "pstack budget", or changing pstack's model choices.

cards.name: sharpen
cards.title: sharpen
cards.description: Make a task deeper, not bigger, then rewrite the prompt. Use for /sharpen.

cards.name: show-me-your-work
cards.title: Show me your work
cards.description: Keep a reviewable decision trail for long-running or unattended work: a TSV log with one row per decision (what, why, evidence, result). Local by default; commit it when a reviewer needs the trail to trust the result. Use for /show-me-your-work, autonomous or multi-phase runs, or work a human reviews after stepping away.

cards.name: statechart
cards.title: Statechart
cards.description: Check a TLA+ model of a system that moves between states, such as a product flow, a protocol, or a service, and draw it as a Mermaid statechart. The report gives the shortest path to each state that breaks a rule. Use for /statechart, or to show a bug as a path through states.

cards.name: swarm
cards.title: Swarm
cards.description: Fan out N parallel workers, drain them, and return one report. Use for /swarm, 'swarm this', or parallel coverage, races, gauntlets, and exploration.

cards.name: tdd
cards.title: TDD Bug Fix
cards.description: Use only when the user explicitly asks for TDD, a failing test, or a regression test, OR when the bug has an obvious cheap local test target. Skip when the test path is unclear, expensive, integration-heavy, or not requested.

cards.name: teach
cards.title: Teach
cards.description: Explain a body of work plainly so a person actually understands it. Runs the `how` and `why` skills and weaves what they find into one clear explanation. Use for 'teach me this', 'help me really understand X', 'explain this change or subsystem to me'.

cards.name: technical-writing
cards.title: Technical writing
cards.description: Layered technical-writing standard: Diátaxis structure, Google developer style sentences, STE instruction rules, Global English syntax. Use for /technical-writing or when writing or reviewing docs, RFCs, readmes, PR descriptions, or commit messages.

cards.name: typescript-best-practices
cards.title: TypeScript best practices
cards.description: TypeScript best practices. Use when reading or editing any .ts or .tsx file.

cards.name: unslop
cards.title: Unslop
cards.description: Cut AI tells from any writing.

cards.name: why
cards.title: Why
cards.description: Use for 'why does X work this way', 'why we picked Y', design rationale, regressions, postmortems, or data-backed thresholds. Discovers available MCPs and queries each evidence category (source control, issue tracker, long-form docs, real-time chat, infrastructure observability, error tracking, product analytics warehouse) in parallel, then returns a cited read on decisions and tradeoffs. Use how for runtime behavior.

cards.name: authoring-a-skill
cards.title: Authoring or modifying a skill
cards.description: You own the skill's voice.

cards.name: autonomous-run
cards.title: Autonomous run
cards.description: You own the exit condition. Define done, then drive to it without stopping.

cards.name: autopilot-full
cards.title: Autopilot-full
cards.description: You own the verdicts, never the PRs. One owner carries each PR from build to merge, and nothing merges until your swarm, which never wrote the code, has proven the code that lands.

cards.name: autopilot-stack
cards.title: Autopilot-stack
cards.description: Run the Autopilot-full playbook, but do not merge.

cards.name: babysit
cards.title: Babysit
cards.description: You own the merge frontier. Declare a mode, clear one PR at a time, stop where the human's call begins. This playbook replaces Cursor's built-in babysit skill for these requests, so do not route…

cards.name: bug-fix
cards.title: Bug fix
cards.description: You own this task. Plan, review, verify. Delegate investigation and the fix to subagents, stay in the lead. Pick each subagent's reasoning level and fast or standard speed for the job, per the…

cards.name: eval
cards.title: Eval
cards.description: You own the experiment design. Plan, blind, run, synthesize.

cards.name: feature
cards.title: Feature
cards.description: You own the design. Plan, review, verify. Delegate implementation. Stay in the lead.

cards.name: hillclimb
cards.title: Hillclimb
cards.description: You own the metric and the experiment's integrity. Supervise and review. Delegate the attempts. For sustained, iterative improvement of one measurable thing against a target. A one-off fix is Bug fix…

cards.name: investigation
cards.title: Investigation
cards.description: You own the answer. Plan, route, write.

cards.name: multi-phase-plan
cards.title: Multi-phase or multi-PR plan
cards.description: You own the plan, not the code. The plan is a checklist an owner runs box by box and the operator audits from the evidence. The plan is the deliverable. Do not implement.

cards.name: opening-a-pr
cards.title: Opening a PR
cards.description: Invoked at the end of every other playbook.

cards.name: orchestrate
cards.title: Orchestrate
cards.description: You run the program, never the code. Decide which agent does each piece of work, then check what each one produces. For a standing project handed to one coordinator chat: multi-day, many stacked PRs,…

cards.name: pause-safely
cards.title: Pause safely
cards.description: You own a clean stop. Leave a checkpoint a cold-start agent can resume from. This is explicit only. On "keep going", "going to bed, keep going", or "don't stop", do not pause.

cards.name: perf-issue
cards.title: Perf issue
cards.description: You own the measurement story. Plan, review, verify the numbers. Tie every fix to a measurement, don't read source instead of measuring.

cards.name: prototype
cards.title: Prototype
cards.description: You own the design decision, not the code. The prototype is a throwaway instrument. The real build follows Feature.

cards.name: refactoring
cards.title: Refactoring
cards.description: You own the contract. The structure changes. The behavior does not. Distinct from Feature, which adds behavior, and Bug fix, which corrects it.

cards.name: runtime-forensics
cards.title: Runtime forensics
cards.description: You own the diagnosis. Instrument the live process, don't theorize from source. The deliverable is a cited diagnosis, not a fix.

cards.name: session-pickup
cards.title: Session pickup
cards.description: You own the resume point. Read the prior trail, don't redo it.

cards.name: shipping
cards.title: Shipping
cards.description: You own what lands. Verify each PR independently, land only the verified run from the root, then keep your hands off the stack.

cards.name: trace-forensics
cards.title: Trace forensics
cards.description: You own the diagnosis from the artifact.

cards.name: visual-parity
cards.title: Visual parity
cards.description: You own pixel-exact equivalence. The baseline is the spec. You do not touch it. Equivalence is verified by image diff, not by eye.

cards.name: worktree-cleanup
cards.title: Worktree and simulator cleanup
cards.description: 1. Snapshot and audit. Record df -h /, then run scripts/worktree-audit.sh [-b <pr-base-ref>] [repo-path] (principle-build-the-lever). Without -b it checks MERGED against origin/HEAD, so pass -b…

cards.name: comment-sicko
cards.title: Comment Sicko
cards.description: A deranged comment-hater that savors deletion and condemns workaround code.

cards.name: poteto-agent
cards.title: Poteto subagent
cards.description: Delegate subagent for code-writing and helper tasks spawned during a `/poteto-mode` run. Use for delegates, not as the runner for `/poteto-mode` itself. Spawn a fresh `poteto-agent` for each new task, and resume one only in the strict cases that poteto-mode's Subagents section names. Reads the `poteto-mode` skill's `SKILL.md` in full before any work, including its inline Principles index. Substituting `generalPurpose` skips that read and drifts.

about:
gstack turns Claude Code into an engineering team of slash commands. [Garry Tan](https://x.com/garrytan), President and CEO of Y Combinator, built it and uses it every day to ship code while running YC.

### How it works

Each skill plays one role, such as CEO, eng manager, designer, staff reviewer, QA lead, security officer, or release engineer. The skills run in the order of a sprint:

**Think → Plan → Build → Review → Test → Ship → Reflect**

Each step writes something the next step reads. `/office-hours` writes a design doc that `/plan-ceo-review` reads. `/plan-eng-review` writes a test plan that `/qa` picks up. `/review` finds bugs, and `/ship` checks that they are fixed. `/browse` drives a headless Chromium browser so `/qa` can click through the app and take screenshots. `/careful` warns before destructive commands, and `/freeze` blocks edits outside one directory.

### Get started

Clone the repo into `~/.claude/skills/gstack` and run `./setup`. Then try these in order:

1. Run `/office-hours` and describe what you're building.
2. Run `/plan-ceo-review` on a feature idea.
3. Run `/review` on a branch, then `/qa` on a staging URL.

### In this deck

Every card is a skill. The **Sprint** lens lays them out in sprint order.

cards.name: autoplan
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Auto-review pipeline — reads the full CEO, design, and eng review skills from disk
and runs them sequentially with auto-decisions using 6 decision principles. Surfaces
taste decisions (close approaches, borderline scope, codex disagreements) at a final
approval gate. One command, fully reviewed plan out.
Use when asked to "auto review", "autoplan", "run all reviews", "review this plan
automatically", or "make the decisions for me".
Proactively suggest when the user has a plan file and wants to run the full review
gauntlet without answering 15-30 intermediate questions. (gstack)

cards.name: benchmark
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Performance regression detection using the browse daemon. Establishes
baselines for page load times, Core Web Vitals, and resource sizes.
Compares before/after on every PR. Tracks performance trends over time.
Use when: "performance", "benchmark", "page speed", "lighthouse", "web vitals",
"bundle size", "load time". (gstack)

cards.name: browse
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Fast headless browser for QA testing and site dogfooding. Navigate any URL, interact with
elements, verify page state, diff before/after actions, take annotated screenshots, check
responsive layouts, test forms and uploads, handle dialogs, and assert element states.
~100ms per command. Use when you need to test a feature, verify a deployment, dogfood a
user flow, or file a bug with evidence. Use when asked to "open in browser", "test the
site", "take a screenshot", or "dogfood this". (gstack)

cards.name: canary
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Post-deploy canary monitoring. Watches the live app for console errors,
performance regressions, and page failures using the browse daemon. Takes
periodic screenshots, compares against pre-deploy baselines, and alerts
on anomalies. Use when: "monitor deploy", "canary", "post-deploy check",
"watch production", "verify deploy". (gstack)

cards.name: careful
cards.title: /careful — Destructive Command Guardrails
cards.description:
Safety guardrails for destructive commands. Warns before rm -rf, DROP TABLE,
force-push, git reset --hard, kubectl delete, and similar destructive operations.
User can override each warning. Use when touching prod, debugging live systems,
or working in a shared environment. Use when asked to "be careful", "safety mode",
"prod mode", or "careful mode". (gstack)

cards.name: checkpoint
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Save and resume working state checkpoints. Captures git state, decisions made,
and remaining work so you can pick up exactly where you left off — even across
Conductor workspace handoffs between branches.
Use when asked to "checkpoint", "save progress", "where was I", "resume",
"what was I working on", or "pick up where I left off".
Proactively suggest when a session is ending, the user is switching context,
or before a long break. (gstack)

cards.name: codex
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
OpenAI Codex CLI wrapper — three modes. Code review: independent diff review via
codex review with pass/fail gate. Challenge: adversarial mode that tries to break
your code. Consult: ask codex anything with session continuity for follow-ups.
The "200 IQ autistic developer" second opinion. Use when asked to "codex review",
"codex challenge", "ask codex", "second opinion", or "consult codex". (gstack)

cards.name: connect-chrome
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Launch real Chrome controlled by gstack with the Side Panel extension auto-loaded.
One command: connects Claude to a visible Chrome window where you can watch every
action in real time. The extension shows a live activity feed in the Side Panel.
Use when asked to "connect chrome", "open chrome", "real browser", "launch chrome",
"side panel", or "control my browser".

cards.name: cso
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Chief Security Officer mode. Infrastructure-first security audit: secrets archaeology,
dependency supply chain, CI/CD pipeline security, LLM/AI security, skill supply chain
scanning, plus OWASP Top 10, STRIDE threat modeling, and active verification.
Two modes: daily (zero-noise, 8/10 confidence gate) and comprehensive (monthly deep
scan, 2/10 bar). Trend tracking across audit runs.
Use when: "security audit", "threat model", "pentest review", "OWASP", "CSO review". (gstack)

cards.name: design-consultation
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Design consultation: understands your product, researches the landscape, proposes a
complete design system (aesthetic, typography, color, layout, spacing, motion), and
generates font+color preview pages. Creates DESIGN.md as your project's design source
of truth. For existing sites, use /plan-design-review to infer the system instead.
Use when asked to "design system", "brand guidelines", or "create DESIGN.md".
Proactively suggest when starting a new project's UI with no existing
design system or DESIGN.md. (gstack)

cards.name: design-html
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Design finalization: generates production-quality Pretext-native HTML/CSS.
Works with approved mockups from /design-shotgun, CEO plans from /plan-ceo-review,
design review context from /plan-design-review, or from scratch with a user
description. Text actually reflows, heights are computed, layouts are dynamic.
30KB overhead, zero deps. Smart API routing: picks the right Pretext patterns
for each design type. Use when: "finalize this design", "turn this into HTML",
"build me a page", "implement this design", or after any planning skill.
Proactively suggest when user has approved a design or has a plan ready. (gstack)

cards.name: design-review
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Designer's eye QA: finds visual inconsistency, spacing issues, hierarchy problems,
AI slop patterns, and slow interactions — then fixes them. Iteratively fixes issues
in source code, committing each fix atomically and re-verifying with before/after
screenshots. For plan-mode design review (before implementation), use /plan-design-review.
Use when asked to "audit the design", "visual QA", "check if it looks good", or "design polish".
Proactively suggest when the user mentions visual inconsistencies or
wants to polish the look of a live site. (gstack)

cards.name: design-shotgun
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Design shotgun: generate multiple AI design variants, open a comparison board,
collect structured feedback, and iterate. Standalone design exploration you can
run anytime. Use when: "explore designs", "show me options", "design variants",
"visual brainstorm", or "I don't like how this looks".
Proactively suggest when the user describes a UI feature but hasn't seen
what it could look like. (gstack)

cards.name: document-release
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Post-ship documentation update. Reads all project docs, cross-references the
diff, updates README/ARCHITECTURE/CONTRIBUTING/CLAUDE.md to match what shipped,
polishes CHANGELOG voice, cleans up TODOS, and optionally bumps VERSION. Use when
asked to "update the docs", "sync documentation", or "post-ship docs".
Proactively suggest after a PR is merged or code is shipped. (gstack)

cards.name: freeze
cards.title: /freeze — Restrict Edits to a Directory
cards.description:
Restrict file edits to a specific directory for the session. Blocks Edit and
Write outside the allowed path. Use when debugging to prevent accidentally
"fixing" unrelated code, or when you want to scope changes to one module.
Use when asked to "freeze", "restrict edits", "only edit this folder",
or "lock down edits". (gstack)

cards.name: gstack-upgrade
cards.title: /gstack-upgrade
cards.description:
Upgrade gstack to the latest version. Detects global vs vendored install,
runs the upgrade, and shows what's new. Use when asked to "upgrade gstack",
"update gstack", or "get latest version".

cards.name: guard
cards.title: /guard — Full Safety Mode
cards.description:
Full safety mode: destructive command warnings + directory-scoped edits.
Combines /careful (warns before rm -rf, DROP TABLE, force-push, etc.) with
/freeze (blocks edits outside a specified directory). Use for maximum safety
when touching prod or debugging live systems. Use when asked to "guard mode",
"full safety", "lock it down", or "maximum safety". (gstack)

cards.name: health
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Code quality dashboard. Wraps existing project tools (type checker, linter,
test runner, dead code detector, shell linter), computes a weighted composite
0-10 score, and tracks trends over time. Use when: "health check",
"code quality", "how healthy is the codebase", "run all checks",
"quality score". (gstack)

cards.name: investigate
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Systematic debugging with root cause investigation. Four phases: investigate,
analyze, hypothesize, implement. Iron Law: no fixes without root cause.
Use when asked to "debug this", "fix this bug", "why is this broken",
"investigate this error", or "root cause analysis".
Proactively invoke this skill (do NOT debug directly) when the user reports
errors, 500 errors, stack traces, unexpected behavior, "it was working
yesterday", or is troubleshooting why something stopped working. (gstack)

cards.name: land-and-deploy
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Land and deploy workflow. Merges the PR, waits for CI and deploy,
verifies production health via canary checks. Takes over after /ship
creates the PR. Use when: "merge", "land", "deploy", "merge and verify",
"land it", "ship it to production". (gstack)

cards.name: learn
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Manage project learnings. Review, search, prune, and export what gstack
has learned across sessions. Use when asked to "what have we learned",
"show learnings", "prune stale learnings", or "export learnings".
Proactively suggest when the user asks about past patterns or wonders
"didn't we fix this before?"

cards.name: office-hours
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
YC Office Hours — two modes. Startup mode: six forcing questions that expose
demand reality, status quo, desperate specificity, narrowest wedge, observation,
and future-fit. Builder mode: design thinking brainstorming for side projects,
hackathons, learning, and open source. Saves a design doc.
Use when asked to "brainstorm this", "I have an idea", "help me think through
this", "office hours", or "is this worth building".
Proactively invoke this skill (do NOT answer directly) when the user describes
a new product idea, asks whether something is worth building, wants to think
through design decisions for something that doesn't exist yet, or is exploring
a concept before any code is written.
Use before /plan-ceo-review or /plan-eng-review. (gstack)

cards.name: plan-ceo-review
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
CEO/founder-mode plan review. Rethink the problem, find the 10-star product,
challenge premises, expand scope when it creates a better product. Four modes:
SCOPE EXPANSION (dream big), SELECTIVE EXPANSION (hold scope + cherry-pick
expansions), HOLD SCOPE (maximum rigor), SCOPE REDUCTION (strip to essentials).
Use when asked to "think bigger", "expand scope", "strategy review", "rethink this",
or "is this ambitious enough".
Proactively suggest when the user is questioning scope or ambition of a plan,
or when the plan feels like it could be thinking bigger. (gstack)

cards.name: plan-design-review
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Designer's eye plan review — interactive, like CEO and Eng review.
Rates each design dimension 0-10, explains what would make it a 10,
then fixes the plan to get there. Works in plan mode. For live site
visual audits, use /design-review. Use when asked to "review the design plan"
or "design critique".
Proactively suggest when the user has a plan with UI/UX components that
should be reviewed before implementation. (gstack)

cards.name: plan-eng-review
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Eng manager-mode plan review. Lock in the execution plan — architecture,
data flow, diagrams, edge cases, test coverage, performance. Walks through
issues interactively with opinionated recommendations. Use when asked to
"review the architecture", "engineering review", or "lock in the plan".
Proactively suggest when the user has a plan or design doc and is about to
start coding — to catch architecture issues before implementation. (gstack)

cards.name: qa
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Systematically QA test a web application and fix bugs found. Runs QA testing,
then iteratively fixes bugs in source code, committing each fix atomically and
re-verifying. Use when asked to "qa", "QA", "test this site", "find bugs",
"test and fix", or "fix what's broken".
Proactively suggest when the user says a feature is ready for testing
or asks "does this work?". Three tiers: Quick (critical/high only),
Standard (+ medium), Exhaustive (+ cosmetic). Produces before/after health scores,
fix evidence, and a ship-readiness summary. For report-only mode, use /qa-only. (gstack)

cards.name: qa-only
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Report-only QA testing. Systematically tests a web application and produces a
structured report with health score, screenshots, and repro steps — but never
fixes anything. Use when asked to "just report bugs", "qa report only", or
"test but don't fix". For the full test-fix-verify loop, use /qa instead.
Proactively suggest when the user wants a bug report without any code changes. (gstack)

cards.name: retro
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Weekly engineering retrospective. Analyzes commit history, work patterns,
and code quality metrics with persistent history and trend tracking.
Team-aware: breaks down per-person contributions with praise and growth areas.
Use when asked to "weekly retro", "what did we ship", or "engineering retrospective".
Proactively suggest at the end of a work week or sprint. (gstack)

cards.name: review
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Pre-landing PR review. Analyzes diff against the base branch for SQL safety, LLM trust
boundary violations, conditional side effects, and other structural issues. Use when
asked to "review this PR", "code review", "pre-landing review", or "check my diff".
Proactively suggest when the user is about to merge or land code changes. (gstack)

cards.name: setup-browser-cookies
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Import cookies from your real Chromium browser into the headless browse session.
Opens an interactive picker UI where you select which cookie domains to import.
Use before QA testing authenticated pages. Use when asked to "import cookies",
"login to the site", or "authenticate the browser". (gstack)

cards.name: setup-deploy
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Configure deployment settings for /land-and-deploy. Detects your deploy
platform (Fly.io, Render, Vercel, Netlify, Heroku, GitHub Actions, custom),
production URL, health check endpoints, and deploy status commands. Writes
the configuration to CLAUDE.md so all future deploys are automatic.
Use when: "setup deploy", "configure deployment", "set up land-and-deploy",
"how do I deploy with gstack", "add deploy config".

cards.name: ship
cards.title: Preamble (run first)
cards.description:
Ship workflow: detect + merge base branch, run tests, review diff, bump VERSION,
update CHANGELOG, commit, push, create PR. Use when asked to "ship", "deploy",
"push to main", "create a PR", "merge and push", or "get it deployed".
Proactively invoke this skill (do NOT push/PR directly) when the user says code
is ready, asks about deploying, wants to push code up, or asks to create a PR. (gstack)

cards.name: unfreeze
cards.title: /unfreeze — Clear Freeze Boundary
cards.description:
Clear the freeze boundary set by /freeze, allowing edits to all directories
again. Use when you want to widen edit scope without ending the session.
Use when asked to "unfreeze", "unlock edits", "remove freeze", or
"allow all edits". (gstack)

about:
Superpowers is a development method for coding agents by [Jesse Vincent](https://blog.fsck.com/2025/10/09/superpowers/). It is a set of skills plus a startup instruction that makes the agent look for a matching skill before every task. When a skill matches, the agent must follow its workflow.

### How it works

The agent doesn't start by writing code. It runs one pipeline:

1. **brainstorming** asks what you want and writes it up as a design for you to approve.
2. **using-git-worktrees** opens an isolated branch and confirms the tests pass before any change.
3. **writing-plans** breaks the design into 2 to 5 minute tasks, each with exact file paths and a check.
4. **subagent-driven-development** hands each task to a fresh subagent and reviews the result.
5. **test-driven-development** makes the agent write a failing test first, and deletes code written before its test.
6. **requesting-code-review** runs between tasks and stops work on any critical issue.
7. **finishing-a-development-branch** runs the tests and offers to merge, open a PR, keep, or discard the branch.

An agent can work through an approved plan alone for a couple of hours.

### Philosophy

Write the test first. Follow a process instead of guessing. Keep the code simple. Verify before you claim success.

### Get started

```
/plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official
```

The skills load on their own, so you can start with a normal request.

### In this deck

Every card is a skill. The **Sprint** lens lays them out in pipeline order.

cards.name: brainstorming
cards.title: Brainstorming
cards.description: You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, modifying behavior, or planning anything new, in software or out of it (a talk, a business, a renovation).

cards.name: diagnosing-superpowers
cards.title: Diagnosing Superpowers
cards.description: Use when a superpowers session went wrong and your human partner wants to know why — repeated work, ignored plans, stumbles, poor results, a skill that didn't fire, "it took too long", "why is it so expensive", "what is it doing" — or wants to build a bug report for the superpowers maintainers, for the current session or a past one identified by id or path, on any harness.

cards.name: dispatching-parallel-agents
cards.title: Dispatching Parallel Agents
cards.description: Use when facing 2+ independent tasks that can be worked on without shared state or sequential dependencies

cards.name: executing-plans
cards.title: Executing Plans
cards.description: Use when executing an implementation plan in the current session as the implementer yourself — your human partner chose inline execution, or no subagent tool is available

cards.name: finishing-a-development-branch
cards.title: Finishing a Development Branch
cards.description: Use when implementation is complete, all tests pass, and you need to decide how to integrate the work

cards.name: receiving-code-review
cards.title: Code Review Reception
cards.description: Use when receiving code review feedback, before implementing suggestions, especially if feedback seems unclear or technically questionable - requires technical rigor and verification, not performative agreement or blind implementation

cards.name: requesting-code-review
cards.title: Requesting Code Review
cards.description: Use when completing tasks, implementing major features, or before merging to verify work meets requirements

cards.name: subagent-driven-development
cards.title: Subagent-Driven Development
cards.description: Use when executing implementation plans with independent tasks in the current session

cards.name: systematic-debugging
cards.title: Systematic Debugging
cards.description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes

cards.name: test-driven-development
cards.title: Test-Driven Development (TDD)
cards.description: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code

cards.name: using-git-worktrees
cards.title: Using Git Worktrees
cards.description: Use when starting feature work that needs isolation from current workspace or before executing implementation plans - ensures an isolated workspace exists via native tools or git worktree fallback

cards.name: using-superpowers
cards.title: The Rule
cards.description: Use when starting any conversation - establishes how to find and use skills, requiring skill invocation before ANY response including clarifying questions

cards.name: verification-before-completion
cards.title: Verification Before Completion
cards.description: Use when about to claim work is complete, fixed, or passing, before committing or creating PRs - requires running verification commands and confirming output before making any success claims; evidence before assertions always

cards.name: writing-plans
cards.title: Writing Plans
cards.description: Use when you have a spec or requirements for a multi-step task, before touching code

cards.name: writing-skills
cards.title: Writing Skills
cards.description: Use when creating new skills, editing existing skills, or verifying skills work before deployment

about:
This is Anthropic's official skills repository. It holds reference skills that show what the skills system can do, from creative work and web testing to MCP servers and internal comms. Anthropic provides them for demonstration and education.

### How a skill works

A skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file. Its frontmatter carries a `name` and a `description`. The agent reads only those two fields at startup. When a task matches the description, it loads the rest of the file.

This is progressive disclosure. The body gives the workflow. Bundled scripts, templates, and reference files load only when the workflow points to them. A skill stays cheap until it is used.

### Philosophy

Teach the agent a repeatable way to do one kind of task. Keep the instructions in a file anyone can read and edit. Let the description decide when the skill loads.

### Get started

```
/plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills
```

Then pick `example-skills` to install most of this deck. `claude-api`, `academy-guide`, and `discernment-nudge` install as their own plugins. After that, mention a skill by name or describe the task.

### In this deck

Every card is a skill. They are independent, so the cards have no links between them. The **Sprint** lens groups them into Build, Design, Write, and Meta.

The repo also ships `docx`, `pdf`, `pptx`, and `xlsx`. Those four are source-available, not open source, so this deck deliberately leaves them out.

cards.name: academy-guide
cards.title: Claude Academy guide
cards.description: Stop and check this skill before finishing any reply to a question about how to use Claude or a Claude product — it recommends matching courses, tutorials, and use cases from Claude Academy (academy.claude.com), Anthropic's learning hub. Trigger on: "how do I", "how can I", "getting started with", "what can Claude do", "teach me", "learn to use"; questions about artifacts, projects, skills, plugins, connectors, MCP; requests about rolling Claude out to a team, class, or organization; and any ask for training materials, onboarding content, or learning resources. Use it when the user is learning how to use a feature or product — not when they are mid-task and just want the task done. This skill composes with other skills: after consulting product documentation to answer how a Claude feature works, also check here for a matching course or tutorial — a docs-grounded answer and an Academy recommendation belong together. Only recommend on a strong match; never invent Academy content.

cards.name: algorithmic-art
cards.title: ALGORITHMIC PHILOSOPHY CREATION
cards.description: Creating algorithmic art using p5.js with seeded randomness and interactive parameter exploration. Use this when users request creating art using code, generative art, algorithmic art, flow fields, or particle systems. Create original algorithmic art rather than copying existing artists' work to avoid copyright violations.

cards.name: brand-guidelines
cards.title: Anthropic Brand Styling
cards.description: Applies Anthropic's official brand colors and typography to any sort of artifact that may benefit from having Anthropic's look-and-feel. Use it when brand colors or style guidelines, visual formatting, or company design standards apply.

cards.name: canvas-design
cards.title: DESIGN PHILOSOPHY CREATION
cards.description: Create beautiful visual art in .png and .pdf documents using design philosophy. You should use this skill when the user asks to create a poster, piece of art, design, or other static piece. Create original visual designs, never copying existing artists' work to avoid copyright violations.

cards.name: claude-api
cards.title: Building LLM-Powered Applications with Claude
cards.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

cards.name: discernment-nudge
cards.title: Discernment nudge
cards.description: After you give a substantive answer or draft that the user may act on — advice or recommendations, drafted artifacts such as goals, plans, pitches, proposals, or emails, estimates or projections, analysis or interpretation of data, factual claims they may rely on, or a multi-step argument — invoke this skill BEFORE finalizing your reply and then, if it applies, append 2-3 short follow-up questions, each tied to something specific in what you just produced, that help the user check key facts, probe the reasoning or assumptions, and notice missing context. Do this at most once per conversation. Skip it when the user asked a trivial how-to or simple lookup, wants a purely educational explanation, asked you only to format, convert, or assemble a file from content they provided, is writing code they will run, is doing creative writing or casual chat, or already asked you to double-check, cite, or review — the skill file explains these boundaries and the exact output format.

cards.name: doc-coauthoring
cards.title: Doc Co-Authoring Workflow
cards.description: Guide users through a structured workflow for co-authoring documentation. Use when user wants to write documentation, proposals, technical specs, decision docs, or similar structured content. This workflow helps users efficiently transfer context, refine content through iteration, and verify the doc works for readers. Trigger when user mentions writing docs, creating proposals, drafting specs, or similar documentation tasks.

cards.name: frontend-design
cards.title: Frontend Design
cards.description: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.

cards.name: internal-comms
cards.title: When to use this skill
cards.description: A set of resources to help me write all kinds of internal communications, using the formats that my company likes to use. Claude should use this skill whenever asked to write some sort of internal communications (status reports, leadership updates, 3P updates, company newsletters, FAQs, incident reports, project updates, etc.).

cards.name: mcp-builder
cards.title: MCP Server Development Guide
cards.description: Guide for creating high-quality MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers that enable LLMs to interact with external services through well-designed tools. Use when building MCP servers to integrate external APIs or services, whether in Python (FastMCP) or Node/TypeScript (MCP SDK).

cards.name: skill-creator
cards.title: Skill Creator
cards.description: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.

cards.name: slack-gif-creator
cards.title: Slack GIF Creator
cards.description: Knowledge and utilities for creating animated GIFs optimized for Slack. Provides constraints, validation tools, and animation concepts. Use when users request animated GIFs for Slack like "make me a GIF of X doing Y for Slack."

cards.name: theme-factory
cards.title: Theme Factory Skill
cards.description: Toolkit for styling artifacts with a theme. These artifacts can be slides, docs, reportings, HTML landing pages, etc. There are 10 pre-set themes with colors/fonts that you can apply to any artifact that has been creating, or can generate a new theme on-the-fly.

cards.name: web-artifacts-builder
cards.title: Web Artifacts Builder
cards.description: Suite of tools for creating elaborate, multi-component claude.ai HTML artifacts using modern frontend web technologies (React, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui). Use for complex artifacts requiring state management, routing, or shadcn/ui components - not for simple single-file HTML/JSX artifacts.

cards.name: webapp-testing
cards.title: Web Application Testing
cards.description: Toolkit for interacting with and testing local web applications using Playwright. Supports verifying frontend functionality, debugging UI behavior, capturing browser screenshots, and viewing browser logs.

about:
Compound Engineering is a plugin from [Every](https://every.to), maintained by Kieran Klaassen and Trevin Chow. It is a set of skills built around one loop: brainstorm, plan, build, review, then write down what you learned so the next piece of work starts easier than the last.

### How it works

Most skills hand work to the next one.

1. **ce-brainstorm** turns a vague idea into a right-sized requirements document.
2. **ce-plan** turns the requirements into a structured plan.
3. **ce-work** executes the plan end to end, in a worktree if you want isolation.
4. **ce-code-review** reviews the diff for bugs, regressions, tests, and standards.
5. **ce-commit-push-pr** commits, pushes, and opens the PR. **ce-babysit-pr** carries it to merge.
6. **ce-compound** records the solved problem as a durable learning in the repo.

**lfg** runs the whole chain hands-off from one request. **ce-compound-refresh** later checks the saved learnings against the current code, so they don't go stale.

### Philosophy

Each unit of work should make the next one easier. Planning and review get the most effort, and the lessons are kept in the repo where later runs can read them.

### Get started

```
/plugin marketplace add EveryInc/compound-engineering-plugin
/plugin install compound-engineering
```

Then try `/ce-brainstorm` on an idea, or `/lfg` on a small request.

### In this deck

Every card is a skill. The plugin also ships per-skill reference agents. Their names repeat with different bodies, so they are not cards. The **Sprint** lens lays the skills out from Think to Compound.

cards.name: ce-babysit-pr
cards.title: Babysit a PR
cards.description: Babysits an open GitHub PR until merge-ready, first judging whether an old PR still belongs. Use when asked to watch a PR over time or update an old one — not for one-shot comment resolution or one CI failure. GitHub (incl. Enterprise) only.

cards.name: ce-bakeoff
cards.title: Bake-off
cards.description: Develop independent competing solutions to a defined brief, compare them, and synthesize a winning approach. Use when choosing well requires developing alternatives beyond their current form. Use ce-pov to judge developed material and ce-ideate to discover opportunities.

cards.name: ce-brainstorm
cards.title: Brainstorm a Feature or Improvement
cards.description: Explore vague or ambitious ideas into a right-sized requirements-only unified plan. Use when the user wants to brainstorm or scope what to build. Not for executing already-specified work. Use ce-pov for a verdict on adopting a named external technology.

cards.name: ce-code-review
cards.title: Code Review
cards.description: Review a named diff or PR for bugs, regressions, tests, and standards. Use when asked to review code or when a shipping skill needs a review receipt. Use when asked to apply this review's findings locally. Use ce-resolve-pr-feedback for feedback already left on a PR.

cards.name: ce-commit
cards.title: Git Commit
cards.description: Create a git commit with a clear, value-communicating message. Use when the user asks to commit/save staged or unstaged changes with a repo-appropriate message.

cards.name: ce-commit-push-pr
cards.title: Git Commit, Push, and PR
cards.description: Commit, push, and open a PR. Use when asked to ship/open a PR, or for PR-description-only flows like writing, rewriting, or describing a PR body.

cards.name: ce-compound
cards.title: /ce-compound
cards.description: Document a solved problem as a durable repo learning. Use when verified work produced non-obvious reasoning absent from its final code, tests, or existing docs; avoid routine fixes whose artifacts already explain the lesson.

cards.name: ce-compound-refresh
cards.title: Compound Refresh
cards.description: Refresh the repo's captured learnings against the current codebase. Use when auditing stale, overlapping, superseded, or drifted learnings; avoid general refactor, debugging, or code review unless the learnings store is explicit.

cards.name: ce-debug
cards.title: Debug and Fix
cards.description: Diagnosis loop for bugs and failing behavior. Use when asked to debug or fix failing or slow behavior.

cards.name: ce-doc-review
cards.title: Document Review
cards.description: Review requirements, plans, or specs with role-specific lenses. Use when the user wants to improve an existing planning document.

cards.name: ce-dogfood
cards.title: Dogfood
cards.description: Hands-off, diff-scoped browser QA of the active branch: maps user flows, drives a real browser, autonomously fixes small breakages with regression tests and commits, judges experience against product personas, and writes a durable dogfood report. Manual invocation only.

cards.name: ce-explain
cards.title: Explain How and Why
cards.description: Explain how and why something has its current shape, or what happened over a window of work, grounded in evidence. Use when the user asks for an explanation. Use ce-pov for a judgment or recommendation.

cards.name: ce-handoff
cards.title: Handoff
cards.description: Create a session handoff for another agent, or resume, find, and read any user-selected continuity source. Use when work or conversation must continue without access to the current session history.

cards.name: ce-ideate
cards.title: Generate Improvement Ideas
cards.description: Generate and evaluate grounded ideas. Use when the user wants ideas, improvements, or surprising directions before choosing one to develop. Not for refining an idea they already have (ce-brainstorm) or judging one already on the table (ce-pov).

cards.name: ce-noslop
cards.title: Write without slop
cards.description: Rewrite, check, or draft prose so it carries no AI writing tells, reads plainly on the first read, and keeps every source fact. Use when asked to make writing plainer or free of those tells, to check writing for them, or when drafting from supplied content. Use ce-promote for channel-specific marketing copy.

cards.name: ce-optimize
cards.title: Optimize a measurable target
cards.description: Optimize a named target with a measured loop: attribute a workload's cost, or score variants and keep winners. Use when a working system's metric should move and the winning change is not already known. Use ce-debug when the job is diagnosis; use ce-work when the change is already known.

cards.name: ce-plan
cards.title: Create Technical Plan
cards.description: Create structured plans for multi-step work, including software and non-software tasks. Use when asked to plan, break down implementation, plan from requirements, or deepen an existing plan; prefer ce-brainstorm for exploratory framing.

cards.name: ce-polish
cards.title: Polish
cards.description: Polish a working feature through user-directed live browser feedback. Use when a functional feature needs focused UX refinement before shipping.

cards.name: ce-pov
cards.title: Form a Point of View
cards.description: Judge a supplied subject against the project's evidence and constraints. Use when assessing an external-adoption question, a holistic take on a document, or a supplied approach set. Use for an oracle panel to consult other models and reconcile their opinions. Use ce-explain for understanding and ce-doc-review for findings review.

cards.name: ce-product-pulse
cards.title: Product Pulse
cards.description: Generate time-windowed product pulse reports from configured signals.

cards.name: ce-promote
cards.title: Promotion Copy
cards.description: Draft launch or promotion copy for a shipped feature.

cards.name: ce-proof
cards.title: Proof - Collaborative Markdown Editor
cards.description: Publish, read, comment on, or edit markdown in Proof. Use for Proof links, sharing specs/plans/drafts, or publish handoffs from planning workflows; avoid proofread, math, evidence, or proof-of-concept meanings.

cards.name: ce-prototype
cards.title: Prototype
cards.description: Build a throwaway prototype to answer how something should work, feel, or read. Use when committing the wrong answer would be expensive to unravel and a cheap sketch cannot settle it. Not a rough visual probe during brainstorming, not for deciding what to build, not polishing a feature that already works, not implementing the real thing.

cards.name: ce-resolve-pr-feedback
cards.title: Resolve PR Review Feedback
cards.description: Judge PR feedback centrally, apply valid fixes, and complete review conversations with publication verified. Use when addressing feedback already left on a PR, preparing local fixes for a caller to publish, or completing a saved feedback batch. Use ce-code-review for reviewing code before feedback exists.

cards.name: ce-retune
cards.title: Retune a Corpus for a New Model
cards.description: Retune a skill corpus for a new model, measurement-first: mine the run archive for a baseline, establish a noise floor, audit the corpus adversarially, then cut in measured passes until a pre-registered bar clears. Requires a benchmark harness that can A/B two builds of the corpus; refuses without one.

cards.name: ce-riffrec-feedback-analysis
cards.title: Riffrec Feedback Analysis
cards.description: Analyze recorded product feedback into evidence for bugs and requirements. Use when a Riffrec capture or other screen, voice, or notes artifact needs interpretation. Use for Riffrec setup, capture, or sharing help when no recording exists yet.

cards.name: ce-setup
cards.title: Compound Engineering Setup
cards.description: Check Compound Engineering health and repo-local config, or scaffold a Compound Pack with `pack:<id>`.

cards.name: ce-simplify-code
cards.title: Mode
cards.description: Simplify code for clarity, reuse, quality, and efficiency while preserving behavior, and prune tests and comments that carry no value. Use after implementation and before review, or to audit tests or comments in any part of a repo; use ce-debug for bugs.

cards.name: ce-strategy
cards.title: Product Strategy
cards.description: Create or update STRATEGY.md. Use when starting a product, adding a strategy doc, or changing direction or roadmap.

cards.name: ce-sweep
cards.title: Feedback Sweep
cards.description: Sweep configured feedback sources (Slack, GitHub Issues; email experimental) for new items: acknowledge at source, analyze recordings, verify fixes merged to main, and emit an `lfg`-ready plan. First run sets up sources; supports mode:non-interactive for scheduled runs.

cards.name: ce-test-browser
cards.title: Browser Test Skill
cards.description: Run browser tests for pages affected by the current branch or PR. Use when asked to run or check browser tests for the current change.

cards.name: ce-test-xcode
cards.title: Xcode Simulator Test
cards.description: Test iOS apps in a simulator with XcodeBuildMCP. Use when iOS changes need simulator evidence before handoff.

cards.name: ce-work
cards.title: Work Execution Command
cards.description: Execute a plan or concrete work prompt end-to-end. Use when implementing from a plan document, a spec path, or a clear build request; use ce-debug for open-ended bugs. Use when an outer orchestrator needs implementation and local verification only, without the shipping tail.

cards.name: ce-worktree
cards.title: Worktree Isolation
cards.description: Set up isolated git worktrees — create a new branch for fresh work, or attach a worktree to an existing branch, PR, or commit. Use when starting isolated work or isolating an existing ref.

cards.name: lfg
cards.title: The run (routes that change the code)
cards.description: Take a request all the way to done, hands-off, through the right Compound Engineering skills. A code change ends as an open pull request, pushed without stopping. Use only when the user explicitly asks for autonomous end-to-end work or invokes lfg directly. Use ce-plan, ce-work, ce-debug, or ce-commit-push-pr for work the user reviews step by step.

cards.name: wtf
cards.title: wtf
cards.description: Explain the last message, or a supplied file, link, or passage, in plain language a person follows on the first read. Use when the user invokes wtf because they did not follow something. Use ce-explain to investigate how or why code works, and ce-noslop to rewrite prose.
